variants.headline: Allies join the war against {{opponent}}
body: {{allies}} have joined the war against {{opponent}}, honoring the pact between us. Their first columns reached our camps this week, and the quartermaster has cleared a second row of stalls for their horses. {{opponent}} must now watch more than one border.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: A warning for our other rivals
body: {{opponent}} now faces another army, because {{allies}} have answered our pact. A promise is only ink until someone calls it in, and this one has been called in the open. Every other court will be recalculating what its own promises are worth.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: The pact answered in arms
body: Letters from the capital relate that {{allies}} have taken up arms beside us against {{opponent}}, as the treaty bound them to do. At the frontier post, the gatekeeper has chalked their colors on the board beside ours. A promise kept in a hard season is the kind worth making in a calm one.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Hear it! We do not fight alone
body: Word of the war, and good word at that! {{allies}} have answered the pact and march with us against {{opponent}}! We do not stand alone! We do not stand alone! Tell every street and every gate!{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Barbarians in sight of {{cityName}}
body: Raiders have come down from the hills within sight of {{cityName}}, {{barbarians}} by the last count. The watch counted them from the tower at dusk, and the outlying farms have emptied into the town. The garrison has barred the north gate and sent word to the nearest camp.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Raiders at the walls
body: Raiders in the hills, {{barbarians}} by the last count! Bring the herds inside before dark and bar the shutters! Mind the children, mind the gate! {{barbarians}} at our door, and the walls are ours to hold!

variants.headline: The herdsmen reach {{cityName}} without the herds
body: The drovers reached the gate at a run on Tuesday, and the cattle did not come with them. The raiders are camped within reach of {{cityName}}, {{barbarians}} by the last count, close enough that their fires show over the ridge. "We left the herd in the field," one said. "Better the herd than us."

variants.headline: Counting raiders at {{cityName}}
body: The raiders number {{barbarians}}, the first figure the scouts around {{cityName}} have agreed on all season. A band that size cannot feed itself in one valley for long; it strips the land and moves on, burning what it cannot carry. Driving it off will take men the harvest can ill spare, and that is the bill the count does not show.

variants.headline: At {{cityName}}, the garrison answers: {{posture}}
body: The town book records raiders in the lands of {{cityName}}, {{barbarians}} by the watch's count. The captain of the watch answered before the day was out, and his order stands in the margin as {{posture}}. The outer farms were brought within the wall, and the gate was shut at dusk.

variants.headline: {{city}} goes hungry under siege
body: {{city}} is under siege, and the city has begun to starve. At the grain exchange a porter says the sacks sold this morning were half chaff, and buyers carried them off without a word. What was thrown away last year is now dinner.

variants.headline: Who can still buy supper in {{city}}?
body: Hunger in {{city}} will not fall evenly, and the siege will find the poorest tables first. A family that buys flour by the day has nothing to fall back on, while a merchant with a cellar can wait a month. The stalls in the market still hold food; the question is whose coin can still reach it.

variants.headline: In {{city}}, the queue starts before dawn
body: {{terms.civic.people}} of {{city}}, the siege has reached the baker's counter. The line forms before dawn now, and the baker weighs each loaf in his hand before he hands it over. Ask him what he will sell when the flour is gone, and he will tell you the truth: nothing.

variants.headline: To the faithful of {{city}}: hold fast
body: To the faithful in this besieged city: the granaries are low and the gates must stay shut. Open the shrines, bring your spare bread to the poor, and let no neighbor face the night alone. What we give up now will be counted in a better season.

variants.headline: The walls of {{cityName}} are failing
body: The walls of {{cityName}} have been broken down to {{hitPoints}} of their {{maxHitPoints}} strength. From the ridge our scouts can see the gap where the masonry fell, and the rubble below it is deep enough to bury a cart. Another push may finish what the last one began.

variants.headline: An accounting of {{cityName}}
body: City: {{cityName}}.
Wall and gate: {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} still standing.
The account: more lost than kept.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight: heavy damage at {{cityName}}
body: Word from abroad tonight: the walls of {{cityName}} are badly damaged. They stand at {{hitPoints}} of their {{maxHitPoints}} strength. The city is still held, but the breach is wide enough to see from the road.

variants.headline: The walls of a rival come down
body: {{cityName}} belongs to {{civilization}}, and its walls now stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}. A wall that low no longer keeps an army out; it only slows one down. Our officers have been waiting for a gap like this, and the next assault will test whether the defenders have anything left behind it.

variants.headline: Our forces attack before {{cityName}}
body: The attack on {{cityName}} opened at dawn, and the men of {{civilization}} on the wall heard our teams hitching up before they saw them. The word along our line is {{posture}}. Whatever the wall answers, the waiting is over.

variants.headline: From {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, by arithmetic
body: A new order is in force before {{cityName}}: {{posture}} has replaced {{previousPosture}}. Staff officers do not change such words for decoration; someone has weighed the men, the stores and the wall, and found the balance favorable. The defenders may draw their own conclusion from the arithmetic.

variants.headline: The offensive at {{cityName}}, entered
body: The scribe of the campaign writes that our army before {{cityName}}, a city of {{civilization}}, began its assault in this season. The command issued that day reads {{posture}}. By evening the forward camp had been struck, and the wagons stood ready behind the lines.

variants.headline: The war moves to {{civilization}}'s streets
body: The attack on {{cityName}} has begun, and the men who marched past the market this morning did not stop for the usual jokes. A water seller at the gate says they drank and said nothing. When soldiers stop talking, the bill is about to be presented.

variants.headline: Back in the fight near {{cityName}}
body: After a season of falling back, our troops before {{cityName}} have been ordered forward against {{civilization}} once more. The new word in the order book is {{posture}}. Wagons that had been sent to the rear are being turned around, and the camps are filling again.

variants.headline: The pullback ends at {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} saw our line pull back; it now sees it return under the word {{posture}}. Officers do not spend a winter falling back for the pleasure of it. They do it to shorten their supply line, and they come forward again when the enemy's has grown longer.

variants.headline: Our forces are back at the line near {{cityName}}
body: At {{cityName}} tonight, our troops are back at the front. The word from command is {{posture}}. The roads that were quiet last week are full of wagons again.

variants.headline: The second try at {{cityName}}
body: The men before {{cityName}} are going forward again, and the {{terms.civic.government}} calls it a resumption. The families who sent those men out the first time may call it something else. Before another levy is raised, let the council show what the pullback gained and who paid for it.

variants.headline: The line comes back from {{cityName}}
body: Before {{cityName}}, a city of {{civilization}}, our forces have gone from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The tents came down before dawn, and the wounded were loaded first. The enemy on the wall let the column go without a shot.

variants.headline: The withdrawal before {{cityName}}
body: The order before {{cityName}} has changed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, and the army has given ground. An order like that is made by a person, at a price, for a purpose, and the ministers have published none of the three. The men who paid for that ground deserve a plainer answer than silence.

variants.headline: Letters from the front: {{cityName}}
body: Letters from the front relate that our forces before {{cityName}} have gone from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The dispatch was four lines long and named no reason for the change. We print the four lines, and we wait with our readers for the rest.

variants.headline: The boys are off the front at {{cityName}}
body: At the tram stop this morning, a woman read the notice twice and then sat down on the bench. Her son's company is one of those coming back from {{cityName}}, and she had not known it until the board told her. The {{terms.civic.government}} will have its reasons for the withdrawal; she has a chair to set at the table.

variants.headline: Enemy colors near {{cityName}}
body: Soldiers wearing the colors of {{enemies}} have been seen within reach of {{cityName}}. Their cooking fires show after dark from the watchtower, and the miller has carried his flour inside the wall. The roads out of town are still open, but few are using them.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! The enemy is near
body: Enemy troops in sight of the walls! {{enemies}} are on the road, and the watch has seen their colors! Stand to your posts, keep the roads clear for the army, and let no one stray beyond the gate! Stand to your posts!

variants.headline: Three things an army near {{cityName}} can do
body: {{enemies}} have brought troops within a day's march of {{cityName}}. From the wall, our officers can see enough to know the force is not a raiding party. An army that size can besiege the walls, burn the fields, or pin the garrison while it strikes elsewhere. Our officers should be asking which of the three it means to do.

variants.headline: Enemy troops just showed up near {{cityName}}
body: Enemy troops near our city. The flags: {{enemies}}. All of them at war with us, all of them this close.

variants.headline: {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} destroyed in the field
body: The recent fighting cost the enemy {{count|unit|units}}, all of them from the same enemy. Our men have stacked the captured standards by the gate, where they lean in a row taller than a man. The enemy will need more than a season to replace what it left behind.

variants.headline: The enemy's losses, counted
body: Enemy units destroyed: {{count}}.
Flags among them: one.
The fighting this season: charged to the enemy.

variants.headline: {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} destroyed in the fighting
body: The front, tonight. Our forces have destroyed {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} in the latest fighting. Every one of them marched under the same flag.

variants.headline: Hear it! {{count|enemy unit|enemy units}} destroyed
body: Count them in the square! {{count}} of the enemy's units broken by our arms! Banners enough to fill a cart, and the enemy knows the count as well as we do! Sing it in the taverns and shout it at the gates!

variants.headline: A capital falls, far from home
body: A foreign capital has fallen to conquest, {{distance}} from the nearest city of ours. Word came in with a spice cargo, and the harbormaster has already asked what the change means for the tariffs. The fighting is far away, but the ledgers that follow it are not.

variants.when: cityName !== null && loser !== null && winner !== null
variants.headline: After {{cityName}} falls, where do the envoys go?
body: {{cityName}} was the seat of {{loser}} and is now held by {{winner}}. A government can lose its capital and keep its authority, or keep the buildings and lose the authority, and the difference is seen in where ambassadors call. Watch the doors that receive them this month.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital
body: In the annals of this year, {{winner}} took the capital of {{loser}} by force of arms, {{distance}} from our own cities. At the shrine, the keeper of the rolls entered the fall in the same hand he used for plagues and comets. The congregation was told to pray for the city's people, and the record does not say why the seat was brought low.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight, a capital has fallen
body: News from abroad tonight: {{winner}} has taken a capital. The city stands {{distance}} from our nearest city. The maps will be reprinted, and the envoys will be busy by morning.

variants.headline: Peace near our borders
body: {{initiator}} and {{target}} have stopped fighting. The nearer of the two sits {{nearest}} from our nearest city, close enough that our carters use the same roads. The toll keepers have stopped asking travelers for their business.

variants.headline: Neighbors at peace again
body: Word reaches us that {{initiator}} and {{target}} have laid down their arms, and that the settlement asked no visible price of either. At the frontier bridge, the barrier stands open and the keeper has swept a winter's leaves from the planks. May the peace prove dull, and may it last longer than the quarrel.

variants.headline: The quiet between {{initiator}} and {{target}}
body: Neither {{initiator}} nor {{target}} gained a term worth printing, and their war is over. Such endings are less mysterious than they look: one treasury or the other reached the bottom of its purse, and the fighting stopped when the money did. The peace costs both sides less than another campaign would have.

variants.headline: When the neighbors' fire burns low
body: The two loud houses have gone quiet, and the lane sleeps. So it is with {{initiator}} and {{target}}.

variants.headline: War breaks out near our borders
body: {{initiator}} has opened a war against {{target}}. The nearer of the two sits {{nearest}} from our nearest city, and the border market has already lost half its stalls. Our farmers will sell closer to home this season.

variants.headline: A war next door
body: The fighting between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has opened {{nearest}} from our nearest city. Distance is the only thing that keeps a war foreign, and that distance is short. Our envoys should be in both camps before the first foraging party crosses our line.

variants.headline: {{initiator}} at war with {{target}}
body: War close to home tonight: {{initiator}} has declared against {{target}}. Our country is not in this fight. At the coach station, the board still lists the eastern route, and the driver will not say whether he means to run it.

variants.headline: Their war, our doorstep
body: Mark this, {{terms.civic.people}}: {{initiator}} and {{target}} are at war, {{nearest}} from fields our families plough. Great powers do not ask leave of the small farmer when they march, and the harvest does not move out of their way. The {{terms.civic.government}} should say now whether our roads and our sons are part of this quarrel.

variants.headline: A war nearby, set down
body: The border record notes that {{initiator}} made war upon {{target}} in this season, and that the nearer of the two lies {{nearest}} from our lands. The warden of the border stone has opened his gate an hour later each morning since the news came. He gives no reason, and the record gives none for him.

variants.headline: A capital falls near our own border
body: {{winner}} has taken a capital from {{loser}}, and the fighting came close enough that our own border guard watched the flag go up. Smoke was visible from the ridge road for two days. The war has come to our doorstep, and we have a new neighbor to learn.

variants.headline: What {{winner}}'s capture means here
body: {{winner}} now holds the capital it took from {{loser}}, and with it the machinery that made {{loser}} a state. Tax rolls, roads and treaties follow the seat, not the flag that used to fly over it. Our own border has a new weight pressing on it, whether or not a stone has moved.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital near our borders
body: In this season {{winner}} took the capital of {{loser}} by the sword, and the city fell near our own marches. Our grandmothers told stories of that gate, and the telling has not improved with the years. The map in the town hall will need a new name in the old place.

variants.headline: A capital just fell near us
body: {{winner}} just took a capital from {{loser}}. Close to home. The neighbor got bigger; we did not.

variants.headline: A town changes hands near our border
body: A town across the border has been taken by force, {{distance}} from the nearest city of ours. The first cart through the gate carried a receipt with an unfamiliar seal. Our farmers have not stopped watching the road.

variants.when: cityName !== null && loser !== null && winner !== null
variants.headline: {{cityName}} falls to {{winner}}
body: {{cityName}} has passed from {{loser}} to {{winner}}, {{distance}} from our nearest city. A town that size brings its market, its mill and its road tax with it, and all of them now face a different capital. The first question for us is not who won, but who will keep the road open.

variants.headline: Notice from abroad: {{cityName}}
body: Notice to travelers and merchants: {{cityName}}, {{distance}} from our cities, now belongs to {{winner}} by right of conquest. Papers bearing the old seal will not be honored at its gate. Those with business there should apply for new ones before the market day.

variants.headline: A new flag {{distance}} out
body: The next town over is under a new flag: {{winner}} has taken it from {{loser}}, {{distance}} from our own streets. The baker there has a new ruler and the same ovens. Our border villages will be the first to find out what that means at the fence.

variants.headline: {{neighbor}}'s army now outranks ours
body: {{neighbor}} now keeps a larger army than we do. The drills on the far side of the border run later than ours, and the sound carries across the valley at night. Nothing has been said at the gate, and nothing needs to be.

variants.headline: The tally of arms
body: The neighbor's strength: {{theirStrength}}.
Our strength: {{ourStrength}}.
The heavier scale: theirs, and only lately.

variants.headline: Ask why {{neighbor}}'s army passed ours
body: {{terms.civic.people}}, the army of {{neighbor}} is now the larger one, and the {{terms.civic.government}} has offered no word on how that came about. It did not happen in a night; it happened in the nights nobody was counting. Ask the sentries what they hear after dark, and ask the council why they never asked.

variants.headline: The balance of arms has turned
body: Set down in the garrison roll: the host of {{neighbor}} has passed ours in strength. The frontier garrison sent its muster to the capital this season with a new column ruled and filled. The armorer has taken on a second apprentice, and the record notes the reason without comment.

variants.headline: Our army passes {{neighbor}}'s
body: Our army has passed that of {{neighbor}} in strength. At the border market, a cattle drover has started asking whether the far pasture is safe again. Nobody has told him yes, and nobody has told him no.

variants.headline: Our arms in good order
body: We are informed that our army now exceeds the army of {{neighbor}}. The drill yard has taken on another smith, and the forges there have not been cold for a week. Ministers may point to that glow as the fruit of their care.

variants.headline: Our army just passed {{neighbor}}'s
body: Our army just passed {{neighbor}}'s on the scale. Leads like this have a season, not a lifetime. Spend it or lose it.

variants.headline: The account of strength
body: Ours, by the latest muster: {{ourStrength}}.
Theirs, by the same reckoning: {{theirStrength}}.
The heavier scale: ours, as of this muster.

variants.headline: {{city}} takes heavy damage
body: {{city}} has taken heavy damage in the recent fighting, and its walls stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}. The masons are back on the ramparts before the dust has settled. Repairs will cost the city a season of wages, and the enemy may return before the work is done.

variants.headline: The cost to {{city}}
body: {{city}} now holds its wall at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}, and the question the city should be asking is where the rest went. A wall falls when the men behind it are too few or the order to reinforce comes too late. Someone knows which it was, and the citizens who pay for the wall deserve to know too.

variants.headline: The crack in {{city}}'s wall
body: On Thursday the masons stopped work at the north wall and carried their tools away without a word. The wall stands at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}, and by supper the number was being repeated in {{city}} like a weather report. Nobody needed to be told what it meant.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{city}}! The walls are hurt
body: Word of the walls! The enemy has hit them hard, and they stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}! Every hand to the mending, every eye to the gate! They stand! They stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}!

variants.headline: Our forces counterattack at {{cityName}}
body: At {{cityName}}, our command has changed the word from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The companies that held the wall are filing out through the postern, and the guns have been hauled around. The enemy camp is about to learn that the town can bite.

variants.headline: From defense to the strike at {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} has held through the word {{previousPosture}} and now takes up {{posture}}. An army that has been on the defensive for a season knows the enemy's habits better than the enemy knows its own. The counterstroke is the reward for that patience, and it should be delivered before the enemy can rest.

variants.headline: Our forces attack at {{cityName}}
body: From {{cityName}} tonight: our troops are attacking. The front order has moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. For the first time this season, the firing is going away from the town.

variants.headline: The defense holds and answers
body: Letters from {{cityName}} relate that our command there has changed its orders from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The forward ditch has been deepened, and the guns that guarded the gate have been wheeled out to it. In the steadiness of that change we read the hand of officers who know their business.

variants.headline: The front at {{cityName}} goes defensive
body: At {{cityName}}, the word for the front has changed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The outposts have been pulled back to the wall, and the wagons are being emptied inside the gate. The town is being made ready to be held.

variants.headline: At {{cityName}}, a stance change unexplained
body: Word comes from {{cityName}} that the order {{previousPosture}} has been replaced by {{posture}}. The citadel has vouchsafed no explanation, and our correspondent there was received with great politeness and shown the door. A change of stance in a town under threat is news the public should hear from its officers, not from its sentries.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Our soldiers stand at the walls
body: Listen, townsfolk! The soldiers are leaving the fields and taking their places on the wall. Keep the streets clear, keep the watch, and go about your business quietly. The wall is manned, and the town stands behind it!

variants.headline: The record of {{cityName}}'s front
body: It is set down that the garrison of {{cityName}} put aside the word {{previousPosture}} and took up {{posture}}. The outer posts were called in that same evening, and the gate was barred early. No reason was written beside the order, and none is supplied here.

variants.headline: A war ends in capitulation
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has ended, and it ended in capitulation. The frontier gate opened to the other side's riders before noon, and the first carried a sealed case straight for the capital. The terms have not been published, but one side has clearly bowed.

variants.headline: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is ended
body: A war is dead, the one between {{initiator}} and {{target}}, and it died on its knees. It began with drums and promises, and it ended with a pen in a room where one side sat and the other stood. What remains is the record, and the record is shorter than the marches.

variants.headline: Our war with {{initiator}} ends in capitulation
body: The war that {{initiator}} began against us has ended in capitulation. Which nation now answers to the other will be read in the terms when they are published, and the terms are not yet in print. Until then, the only certain fact is that the fighting has stopped.

variants.headline: Our war with {{target}} is settled
body: A peace with {{target}} has been concluded, and the terms carry a capitulation. On the border road the barrier is down and the first cart in months has crossed without a challenge. We grant that the instrument is a hard one; we are still glad the swords are back in their scabbards.

variants.headline: A peace with visible terms
body: Peace terms were posted at the exchange this noon, with the count of concessions set at {{count}}: {{concessions}}. A wool buyer copied the names into his ledger before he would quote a price. The market has decided to trust the paper, and the paper has not yet been tested.

variants.headline: The terms between {{initiator}} and {{target}}
body: Parties: {{initiator}} and {{target}}.
Terms conceded: {{count}}.
Entered as: {{concessions}}.

variants.headline: Who owes what in the peace with {{target}}?
body: The settlement with {{target}} records concessions of these kinds: {{concessions}}. A concession is either a payment or a promise, and the difference matters to every household that will help pay for it. Let the {{terms.civic.government}} publish the terms in two columns, what we gave and what we received, before it asks for another budget.

variants.headline: A peace with terms tonight
body: {{initiator}} and {{target}} have made peace tonight. The settlement records a concession count of {{count}}. A clerk read the pages aloud at the exchange, and the crowd stayed to hear the list.

variants.headline: Peace on one front only
body: Peace has been made with {{settled}}, and the fighting on that side has stopped. The war with {{remaining}} continues, and the regiments from the quiet front are already on the road. There is no rest for them, only a shorter road to the next fight.

variants.headline: One account closes, others stay open
body: One war is finished and the others are not: {{settled}} has made peace with us, while {{remaining}} has not. A treaty on one border always frees soldiers for another, and the direction they march is a truer statement of policy than any speech. The {{terms.civic.government}} can explain its priorities by where it sends those men.

variants.headline: Peace with {{settled}}
body: The peace with {{settled}} is concluded, and the guns on that front have fallen silent. The bells rang at noon and then stopped, as though the sexton had thought better of rejoicing while other fronts burn. We note with regret that the war with {{remaining}} goes on, and we hope good sense reaches it before the harvest does.

variants.headline: Bells for one front, drums for the others
body: Peace with {{settled}} is signed, and the bells have rung for it. The war with {{remaining}} is not signed, and the same bells will not ring for the families still waiting. Let the {{terms.civic.government}} explain to those families why one front can be closed and another left open.

variants.headline: We are at peace
body: The last war has ended, and no power now stands against us. At the barracks gate, soldiers have stacked their packs and are sitting in the sun with their boots off. The first night without a watch will feel strange to them.

variants.headline: The record of rest
body: In this season the fighting ceased, and the nation had rest from its enemies. The shrines were filled past their doors, and the priests gave thanks for a quiet border. The scribe prays that no later hand will need to amend the entry.

variants.headline: The long walk home
body: At noon the first uniforms came up the market road, and the baker put a loaf into every hand he could reach. Children ran beside the column until their mothers called them back. The peace may have been signed in a distant room, but it arrived here as bread.

variants.headline: Peace, and what to do with it
body: The guns are quiet, and we are glad to say so. The harder work begins now: repair the roads the armies ruined, settle the debts they left, and find places for the men who have no camp to return to. A peace that is only celebrated is a peace half kept.

variants.headline: Please print the names by village
body: Madam, the news says the war is over, and the road home is long. When you have the names of those returning, will you print them village by village? Our mother cannot read a page of print, but she knows one name by its shape, and she has been looking for it a long time.

variants.headline: {{count}} of our companies lost in action
body: The recent fighting cost us {{count|company|companies}}, all of them against the same enemy. At the barracks, the clerk has begun a second page for the names. The town will know most of them before the page is full.

variants.headline: Our losses, counted
body: Companies lost: {{count}}.
Enemy they fell to: one, and the same one throughout.
The cost: entered. The answer: still missing.

variants.headline: The empty bunks
body: On Thursday the landlady at the barracks gate set out fewer plates and said nothing about it. The recent fighting cost us {{count|company|companies}}, all to the same enemy. The street had the number before the newspaper did, and the street had it right.

variants.headline: The count from the fighting
body: They say {{count}} of our companies were lost in the last fighting, and every one to the same foe. The old men by the well tell it the same way, which they seldom do. When the tellers agree, the tale is usually true, and usually bad.

variants.headline: Vassals drawn into the war
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has grown to include {{vassals}}, who march under their oaths. Their columns took the road this week, and the inns along it were full. A quarrel between two powers is now being fought by several.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: What the vassals add
body: {{vassals}} have entered the war between {{initiator}} and {{target}}, as their oaths require. A vassal does not choose the quarrel, only the march, so the names on the list add soldiers without adding a cause. The war has not spread; it has simply grown heavier.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: The record of vassalage honored
body: The book of oaths records that {{vassals}} entered the war between {{initiator}} and {{target}}, being bound by vassalage. Their banners followed the master's road, as such banners did in the reigns before this one. The scribe notes that the oath was kept, and says nothing of what it cost.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Small kings, big wars
body: {{vassals}} are being marched to a war that {{initiator}} and {{target}} began, and nobody thought to ask them. A small power's oath is a fine thing for the great to own and a poor thing for the small to keep. {{terms.civic.people}}, look at who signs these arrangements and who is only named in them.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Our advantage over {{opponent}} stops growing
body: The war against {{opponent}} has stopped moving in our favor. The supply yard still loads flour every morning, but the clerk has begun asking the same provisioners for the same amount twice. Nobody at the front can say when the line last moved.

variants.headline: The stalled advance against {{opponent}}
body: After a run of good reports, the count against {{opponent}} has barely changed. A stalled tally can mean a pause, a siege, or an army that has outrun its wagons, and the record does not yet say which. Until it does, the supply trains will keep rolling to the same camps.

variants.byline: A farmer with a son in the ranks
variants.headline: The war that stands still
body: Madam, the war with {{opponent}} has settled into one place, and my son's regiment has settled with it. The fields are ploughed without him, the taxes are collected without him, and only the fighting has found nothing to do. Will some counselor tell us what the army is waiting for, and how long we are to wait with it?

variants.headline: Stuck: the war with {{opponent}}
body: No movement on the front again this week. Same camps, same bills. A war that stands still keeps charging rent.

variants.headline: Two friends go to war
body: {{first}} and {{second}} are at war, and both of them are friends of ours. Their envoys still greet each other in our capital by name, but they no longer share a carriage to the palace. Friendship with us did not promise them friendship with each other.

variants.headline: When friends fight
body: Our two friends {{first}} and {{second}} are now enemies, and each will want to know what our friendship is worth. Sell to both and arm neither, and both will read the same even hand as a betrayal. There is no neutral answer that either court will call friendly.

variants.headline: A plea in the war of {{first}} and {{second}}
body: It grieves us to write that {{first}} and {{second}}, both friends of this nation, have turned their arms on one another. We will not pretend to judge a quarrel whose beginnings we do not know. We ask only that our good offices be offered to both, before the chairs at the table are broken past mending.

variants.headline: They say the table is broken
body: They tell it by the fire now: {{first}} and {{second}}, who once drank together under our roof, have drawn steel on each other. The old bond, they say, breaks with the loudest crack. The cup they shared is still on the shelf, and the place where it sits has not been dusted since.

variants.headline: The war runs long
body: The war has now run {{turns}}. A carpenter whose two apprentices marched away at the start has stopped telling customers when they will return. He finishes the doors himself now, and he does not talk about it.

variants.headline: The long stretch of the war with {{opponent}}
body: The war with {{opponent}} has run {{turns}}. A war that lasts that long stops being the war its makers declared: the men change, the money changes, and the purpose quietly changes with them. The terms signed at the end will belong to a different quarrel than the one that opened.

variants.headline: The record of a long war
body: The town book notes that the war has stood {{turns}}. A war of that length used to be the work of a grandfather's whole life. In the muster yard, the sergeant is now enrolling young men who were not born when it started.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} is {{turns}} old
body: The war with {{opponent}} has reached {{turns}}, and the bakery has taken down the board it used to mark the count. Nobody at the counter can remember what the quarrel was about at the start. Everybody knows someone who is still out there.

variants.headline: The nation is at war
body: War has come to the nation. At the courthouse, a line has formed at the recruiting table, and the sergeant is taking names in a new book. Out on the frontier, the watch fires are lit while the sky is still pale.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: {{initiator}} has attacked
body: War, tonight. {{initiator}} has declared against us. Our troops are at their posts and the reserves are being called in. We will bring more as it reaches us.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Hear it! {{initiator}} makes war on us
body: Hear it! {{initiator}} has declared war upon us! Every man to his post and every store under lock! We did not ask for this war, and we will answer it!{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: A state of war with {{target}}
body: A state of war now exists between this nation and {{target}}. The {{terms.civic.government}}, we are given to understand, reached its decision only after long deliberation. The first levy has been ordered, and the couriers who carried it were still in the yard when this paper went to press. We trust that the deliberation was as thorough as we are told.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.when: role === 'joined' && reason === 'pact' && initiator !== null && target !== null
variants.headline: Their quarrel, our treaty
body: By treaty, the quarrel between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is now our quarrel. A pact is a promise to pay later, and later has arrived at our door. {{terms.civic.people}}, ask the council what this war is expected to buy, and ask it now, while the ledgers are still open.{{hostileAllies}}

values.attackers: (() => { const declarations = new Map(merge.members.map(({ incident }) => [incident.initiator.id, incident.initiator])); const named = [...declarations.values()].filter(p => p.knows('name')).map(p => p.name); const unknown = declarations.size - named.length; if (unknown) named.push(unknown === 1 ? 'one unnamed power' : unknown + ' unnamed powers'); return named.join(', '); })()
values.otherFronts: (() => { const declarations = merge.members.map(m => m.incident); const fresh = new Set(declarations.map(i => i.initiator.id)); const first = declarations.reduce((a, b) => b.turn < a.turn ? b : a); const earlier = new Set(first.earlierWarOpponents.map(entry => entry.player.id)); const ongoing = [], other = []; for (const rival of self.wars) { if (!rival.knows('major') || !rival.major || !rival.knows('id') || fresh.has(rival.id)) continue; (earlier.has(rival.id) ? ongoing : other).push(rival.knows('name') ? rival.name : 'an unnamed power'); } return [ongoing.length ? 'Already at war with: ' + ongoing.join(', ') + '.' : '', other.length ? 'Other active fronts: ' + other.join(', ') + '.' : ''].filter(Boolean).join(' ') || 'These declarations account for all active major fronts.'; })()
values.allies: (() => { const named = new Map(); for (const { incident } of merge.members) for (const entry of incident.hostileCityStateAllies) if (entry.player.knows('name')) named.set(entry.player.id, entry.player.name); return named.size ? ' Hostile city-state allies: ' + [...named.values()].join(', ') + '.' : ''; })()

variants.headline: War on {{count|front|fronts}}
body: New declarations of war have reached the capital from {{merge.values.attackers}}.{{merge.values.allies}}
{{merge.values.otherFronts}}

variants.headline: War on {{count|front|fronts}}
body: The nation is at war with {{enemies}}. In the map room, each front has its own colored pin, and a clerk keeps a separate ledger for every one. The copying alone takes a full morning now.

variants.headline: Count the fronts
body: We now fight {{count|war|wars}}, against {{enemies}}, and each of them asks for the same men. A soldier sent to one front is a soldier the others do without, and the {{terms.civic.government}} has not said which front matters most. Until it does, the army is being spent in equal portions on unequal quarrels.

variants.headline: Hear it! The nation fights on {{count|front|fronts}}
body: The roll of our enemies: {{enemies}}! The war is wide, so the fields must be wider and the watch longer! Keep the harvest coming and the gates manned! {{enemies}}, hear it, and know we are still standing!

variants.headline: We are at war with {{count|power|powers}} now
body: War count: {{count|power|powers}}. The names: {{enemies}}. One purse pays for all of them. Yours.

variants.headline: The war tally favors {{opponent}}
body: The count in the war with {{opponent}} has fallen to {{score}} in their favor. The printer on the high street still posts each new figure, but fewer people stop to read it. Those who do ask the same question: when will there be talks?

variants.headline: The number nobody in the {{terms.civic.government}} quotes
body: The tally in the war with {{opponent}} now reads {{score}}, and no minister has spoken of the figure in public. Numbers like that are not weather; they are the sum of decisions that were made and orders that were given. The country is entitled to hear how the sum was reached.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} tonight
body: Tonight, the count in the war with {{opponent}} stands at {{score}} against us. Commanders talk about holding the line. No one talks about moving it.

variants.headline: The record of a hard season
body: The campaign book records that the count against {{opponent}} stands at {{score}}. The hospital this season has taken in more wounded than it has beds, and the overflow lies in the cloister. Our fathers had seasons of this kind, and the book has never pretended otherwise.

variants.headline: Our side leads in the war with {{opponent}}
body: The count in the war with {{opponent}} has reached {{score}} on our side. At the post office, a clerk says the same families come every week for letters and every week ask the same question. A good tally has not yet brought anyone home.

variants.headline: What the lead is worth
body: We now lead {{opponent}} by {{score}} on the war's own accounting. A lead of that size is bought with ground and men, and it is worth only what the other side will pay to stop losing. The moment to test that price is while the lead is fresh.

variants.headline: The war proceeds favorably
body: Notice is given that the war with {{opponent}} goes well, with the count at the exchange standing at {{score}} in our favor. Shipping agents at the docks have begun quoting lower rates on the eastern run. Merchants may plan accordingly.

variants.headline: Good news, and the bill beside it
body: The tally against {{opponent}} reads {{score}} in our favor, and the barkeep has written it on the board next to the price of ale. A customer asked whether a number that good would settle his tab. "Numbers don't pour," the keeper said, and filled the glass anyway.

variants.headline: The war sits lighter on the country
body: Weariness with the war has eased to {{weariness}} in a hundred, down from above the halfway mark. On the high street, the talk has turned from the front to the price of roof tiles. The shops are busier than they were a month ago.

variants.headline: Weariness eases in the war with {{opponent}}
body: The public's weariness with the war against {{opponent}} has fallen to {{weariness}} in a hundred. At the coach office, the clerk says passengers have begun asking about the southern road again, and the morning coach has been full all week. A nation that can still look past a war is a nation that can end one.

variants.headline: The number behind the mood
body: The country's weariness with the war against {{opponent}} has dropped to {{weariness}}, after sitting above the halfway mark. A nation's patience is a store like any other, and this one has just been replenished. That store, not a battle, decides how long a war can be fought.

variants.headline: Down to {{weariness}}: the country exhales
body: Still at war. The barber says nobody mentioned the front until noon. First complaint of the day was a haircut.

variants.headline: The war begins to wear us down
body: Weariness with the war against {{opponent}} has reached {{weariness}} in a hundred. A cobbler on the east street says the same boots keep coming back for another sole, and the customers no longer pretend they are buying new. The war is being paid for in small repairs now.

variants.headline: A weary nation, and no statement
body: The country's weariness with the war against {{opponent}} has passed the halfway mark and now stands at {{weariness}}. The {{terms.civic.government}} has said nothing about how it means to answer that mood. Silence in a season like this is read as an answer, and not a reassuring one.

variants.headline: Tired of the war? Say it plainly
body: {{weariness}} in a hundred: that is how far the country's patience has worn in the war against {{opponent}}. A figure like that is not a weather report; it is a vote being taken in kitchens and workshops. Councilors, hear it now, before it is spoken in a way you cannot ignore.

variants.headline: The record of a weary nation
body: The almshouse book records that the nation's weariness with the war against {{opponent}} has reached {{weariness}} in a hundred. The line at the almshouse forms before light now, and the butcher weighs his rations with a heavier hand. A patient people is not an endless one.
